discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: A weak ridge building over the Pacific Northwest will bring a brief break in precipitation today. An active weather pattern resumes early next week with a series of systems moving across Western Washington.
hydrology: The Skokomish River fell below flood stage early this morning and will continue to fall today. The flood warning remains in effect as the flood wave moves down the lower reaches this morning. The river will rise again Sunday night and Monday with the potential for renewed flooding. River flooding is not expected elsewhere over the next 7 days.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A weak ridge building over the Pacific Northwest will bring a brief break in precipitation today. An active weather pattern resumes early next week with a series of systems moving across Western Washington.

sections.title: Short term (today through Monday)
paragraphs: High pressure will lead to dry and stable conditions across western WA today. The low level air mass remains moist with fog and stratus covering much of the lowlands this morning. Mid and high level clouds will increase this afternoon and overall we'll see mostly cloudy skies. Expect highs near 50.

Despite the higher pressure, high tides are still high enough for minor coastal flooding in the interior this morning - a Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect. A Coastal Flood Watch is also in effect for Sunday's high tide (San Juans) with potential for minor to moderate flooding impacts.

Low pressure near 140W will track NE and off the coast on Sunday, then shift inland on Monday bringing more rain and wind to the region. Rain will be mostly light on Sunday, with wetter conditions as the low moves inland on Monday. Snow levels remain fairly high for rain in the Olympics and high-elevation snow in the Cascades (over 4000 ft). Additional rainfall will keep the Skokomish River running high with the potential for renewed flooding. Elsewhere, we're looking at another 1-2" of rain over the coast and up to 1" in the interior through both days. This system will bring more wind too, especially on Monday as the 980-ish low moves in. NBM mean gusts are in the 30s and 40s MPH with high-end gusts reaching the 50s along the coast and NW Interior. And with lower pressure, stronger winds, and rain, there's another threat of coastal flooding in the interior around Monday's high tide. This system weakens and shifts north into B.C. Monday night with rain and wind easing over western WA. 33

sections.title: Long term (Monday night through Friday)
paragraphs: Weak high pressure nudges inland on Tuesday for a break in the weather. However, coastal flooding in the interior still remains a threat due to high astronomical tides. A weak, splitting, system slowly breaks up over the region Wednesday and Thursday for a chance of rain. Low pressure dives to our south late in the week, keeping western WA mainly dry. Temperatures look close to average throughout. 33

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Northwesterly flow aloft shifting southwesterly by this afternoon as an upper level ridge axis traverses the area today. Most terminals reporting light and variable winds this early morning at the surface and these will persist until between 15-18Z before speeds increase to 4-8 kts with a more north to northeasterly direction this afternoon and evening. Light and variable winds returning to most terminals late tonight.

Largely MVFR to IFR conditions across W WA to start the day today as the combination of few clouds aloft and light winds at the surface have allowed for the formation of stratus and fog. Cigs within these categories are fairly consistent across most terminals this morning with the largest variations occuring within visibilities, running the gamut between 1/4SM with FG to P6SM over the past several hours. TAFs leaning pessimistic and given the variability, will likely remain in that vein for the 12Z issuance...the only glimmer of optimism may be to introduce TEMPO groups to where conditions have improved somewhat. Still on track for low level moisture to burn off at most locations by 20Z this afternoon, with widespread VFR conditions returning thereafter. Incoming high clouds in advance of the next weather system entering the area late Sunday may reintroduce cigs to the area tonight, however conditions looking to stay VFR overnight.

KSEA....Conditions bouncing between MVFR and IFR this early morning thanks to low clouds and varying visibilities and conditions likely to remain this way for much of the morning. Conditions becoming more solidly MVFR by 18Z with a return to VFR conditions around the 20- 22Z time frame...remaining that way for the rest of the TAF period. Light and variable winds for much of the morning before becoming predominantly north to northeast with speeds increasing to 4-8 kts.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Winds will remain lighter this morning before east winds develop this afternoon and continue through Sunday. Winds then shift southeast Sunday night ahead of the next storm system. Localized Small Craft Advisory wind gusts may occur Sunday along the western entrance of the Strait of Juan de Fuca and southern coastal waters, however will wait to put forward any headlines to see if these speeds become a little more widespread throughout their respective zones.

A strengthening weather system moves northwards across the Northeast Pacific Sunday and into the Coastal Waters on Monday. Uncertainty continues in regards to the exact track and strength of this weather system. At this time, south winds are expected to peak on Monday. Probabilities show 75 to 95% chance for gale force wind gusts over the Coastal Waters on Monday, with probabilities of 40 to 70% for the interior waters. Winds are expected to be strongest along the coastal waters, and there is a 20 to 40% probability for Storm force wind gusts during this period. Winds begin to ease on Tuesday, but remain elevated at times through the week as additional weather systems are possible.
Seas generally 5 to 8 feet today and Sunday, then increasing with the next system on Monday, ranging 15 to 18 feet. JD/18

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: Dry weather and offshore winds return Saturday. Active weather returns Sunday into Monday with rain and windy conditions. High winds are possible Sunday night into Monday morning, especially along the coast. A break from rain and wind is expected late Tuesday into Wednesday before rain returns Wednesday night into Thursday.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Dry weather and offshore winds return Saturday. Active weather returns Sunday into Monday with rain and windy conditions. High winds are possible Sunday night into Monday morning, especially along the coast. A break from rain and wind is expected late Tuesday into Wednesday before rain returns Wednesday night into Thursday.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Thursday night...Dry weather has returned to NW OR and SW WA for the day as brief ridging moves inland. Mid and upper level clouds dissipated quickly with the rain last night, which lead to perfect conditions for low stratus and fog development across the interior lowlands and portions of the coast. Expect fog/stratus to dissipate by midday, leaving some locations to see some sunshine before high clouds spread inland from south to north this afternoon ahead of the next weather system.

Ensemble guidance is in very good agreement that the next weather system will approach the Oregon coast from the west on Sunday then push northeast toward the Puget Sound/Vancouver Island Sunday night into Monday. This system will bring additional widespread rain Sunday morning into Monday, the potential for light Cascade snow, and increasing southerly winds Sunday night into Monday. The amount of moisture associated with this system is less than the previous two systems. Between 4 AM Sunday and 4 AM Tuesday, there is a 50-75% chance for the interior lowlands to receive at least 1 inch of rain and a 40-70% chance for the coast and terrain to receive at least 2 inches of rain. Rain amounts of this magnitude falling within a 48-hour period suggests flooding is unlikely to occur. Although snow levels will likely fall below the Cascade passes Monday night into Tuesday, precipitation will be winding down at that time. Therefore, forecast snow amounts will most likely only reach a trace to one inch at pass level (70-80% chance for at least 0.1 inches of snow at Willamette and Santiam Passes and 15-20% along highway 26 near Government Camp). Chances for snow amounts over 1 inch are 20-30% over Willamette Pass and less than 5% at passed to the north. Therefore, significant travel impacts are not expected at pass level.

Wind is the primary concern late Sunday night into Monday morning as many ensemble members indicate the surface low strengthening as it approaches and moves north along the coast. The NBM indicates a 40-60% chance of peak wind gusts exceeding 58 mph (High Wind Warning criteria) along the immediate coast and for elevations above 1500 ft in the Coast Range and a 15-30% chance for inland coastal communities such as Astoria and Tillamook. There's also a 20-50% chance for peak wind gusts exceeding 45 mph (Wind Advisory criteria) in the Willamette Valley, Portland/Vancouver metro area, and Cascade foothills and a 60-80% chance over the Coast Range. Gusts of this strength would cause some degree of downed trees and power outages, especially as soils continue to saturate from continued weather systems.

Light showers will continue into Tuesday, mainly over higher terrain and along the coast, as a weak trough originating from Alaska with limited moisture moves through the PacNW. Colder air moves in behind this trough, dropping daytime temperatures into the mid 40s for the interior lowlands for Wednesday through the rest of the week. Additionally, ensembles are confident in a period of dry weather Tuesday night through Wednesday afternoon with the arrival of a transient shortwave ridge. Dry weather is not expected to last long as ensembles indicate another weather system bringing additional precipitation to the area sometime late Wednesday into Thursday. Ensemble guidance shows large model spread for QPF amounts during that time, though even the wettest ensemble guidance suggests flooding will not be a threat. With the cooler temperatures, snow levels will remain below pass level with this system, meaning some snow is possible over the Cascade passes. However, the uncertainty in precipitation amounts leads to uncertainty in snow amounts. Latest NBM indicates a 30-50% chance of at least 0.1 inch of snow over Cascades passes through 4 AM Friday with probabilities decreasing by around 10% with each inch increased. -03

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12Z Sunday...At 1130z Sat, most terminals are experiencing a mix of LIFR/IFR/MVFR CIGs. Guidance indicates fog development is possible again after 13-15z Sat across the Willamette Valley, though there is uncertainty with which terminals will receive fog. Terminals that maintained IFR/MVFR stratus overnight (such as KPDX, KTTD, KSPB, KKLS) may end up not receiving dense fog with only patchy fog or mist developing instead. Models suggest a 50-70% chance for VIS of 1/2SM or lower across the central and southern Willamette Valley at any given hour through 17-19z Sat. After this, conditions should begin to gradually improve with VFR conditions by the early afternoon. An exception could be the southern Valley (KEUG), where northerly winds will help maintain low stratus. Tightening offshore pressure gradients will also support increasing easterly winds across eastern Portland Metro terminals and along the coast with gusts up to 25-30 kts at KTTD after 18-20z Sat.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...CIGs have improved to MVFR, but there is a 40-60% chance for LIFR conditions due to low stratus or fog developing at any given hour through 18z Sat. VFR conditions with high clouds return after 18-20z Sat. Light northwesterly winds under 5 kt will increase and turn easterly to 9-12 kt after 18-21z Sat. -03

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A brief break in active weather will see calmer marine conditions today into early Sunday with seas around 5-8 ft at 11-13 seconds. However, another weather system will impact the waters Sunday afternoon into Monday. There is 70-90% chance of gales Sunday night into Monday, with a brief 25-45% chance of storm force winds Monday morning. A strong west to northwesterly swell then builds over the coastal waters associated with this weather system through Monday afternoon. Confidence is high (65-75% chance) that wave heights exceed 15 ft again Monday at 10-12 seconds, with a 20-40% chance of exceeding 20 ft. Wave heights are expected to decrease below 15 ft by Tuesday morning and will continue to decrease through the day. -03
